strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/6383718d5b3e4989a7970564d2658980/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important and underexplored limitation of video-to-audio systems: generated sound may be perceptually plausible without varying consistently with visible physical dynamics.

PAVAS offers a coherent open-domain pipeline combining object discovery, mass and velocity estimation, object-centric features, and residual physics conditioning. The proposed delta-modulation is technically reasonable and integrates into a strong diffusion-transformer backbone with little parameter overhead.

Evaluation covers distributional quality, semantic alignment, synchronization, a targeted physics benchmark, ablations, and a human study. Against the strongest comparable baseline, MMAudio-L, PAVAS improves most reported objective metrics while preserving synchronization performance.

The ablations include a longer-training control, separate mass and velocity variants, their combination, and direct-summation versus delta-modulation. These results suggest that the added pathways provide benefits beyond simply fine-tuning the backbone for more iterations.

The paper is generally clear and well organized, with informative pipeline and spectrogram figures. VGG-Impact and the attempt to formalize physics-aware V2A evaluation could be useful foundations for subsequent research.
weaknesses: The central physical-realism evidence is not sufficiently validated. APCC compares onset strength with kinetic-energy change computed from the authors' own estimated masses and velocities; PAVAS is conditioned on those same estimates, whereas competing methods are not. A low APCC difference can therefore measure consistency with PAVAS's conditioning signal rather than correctness with respect to real physical quantities. No ground-truth mass, velocity, impact energy, or calibrated acoustic-energy measurements are used.

The physical interpretation of APCC is oversimplified. Recorded onset strength is affected by material, contact geometry and duration, environment, source-to-microphone distance, gain control, and background sound, while only a varying and often small fraction of lost kinetic energy becomes audible energy. The paper neither controls for these confounders nor reports per-class correlations, sample counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or even the ground-truth APCC values. With only 272 moments across ten classes, correlation estimates may be unstable.

The claimed reliability of the Physics Parameter Estimator is crucial but unsupported in the supplied manuscript: its quantitative mass and velocity evaluations are deferred entirely to supplementary material. In particular, metric velocity from an unconstrained monocular video has an inherent absolute-scale ambiguity, yet the paper does not explain how CUT3R's coordinate scale is calibrated to meters. VLM-generated object mass is likewise treated as a reliable measurement without results, uncertainty estimates, or propagation of estimator error.

The ablations do not isolate whether numerical physics is responsible for the gains. Every mass/velocity condition is built by modulating additional masked object-centric visual features, but there is no object-feature-only control, shuffled/random-physics control, oracle-versus-estimated comparison, or robustness analysis under mass and velocity perturbations. Consequently, improvements could arise from object localization and extra visual conditioning rather than meaningful use of physical values.

VGG-Impact is very small and derived from the same VGGSound domain used for physics-aware fine-tuning. Its selection procedure, class distribution, annotation protocol, exclusions, inter-annotator agreement, and benchmark split are insufficiently specified. Broader testing on controlled interactions with known physical parameters or out-of-domain videos is needed to support open-world physical-grounding claims.

The subjective study is under-specified and apparently limited: 15 participants rate 'eight generated audio,' with no clear number of clips per method, sampling protocol, randomization, headphone screening, repeated-measures treatment, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Mean differences over MMAudio-L therefore cannot be judged statistically.

Several reported general-quality gains over MMAudio-L are modest and have no variance across seeds. Comparisons also mix 44.1-kHz PAVAS/MMAudio with predominantly 16-kHz baselines and use author samples for some methods, limiting comparability. PAVAS does not improve DeSync over MMAudio-L, despite the broader wording that it performs favorably across all measures.

Reproducibility is limited by missing prompts, Fourier frequencies, normalization statistics, detailed architecture settings, kinetic-energy and APCC aggregation formulas, impact/onset matching rules, and benchmark annotations. These omissions are more than presentation refinements because they prevent independent reconstruction of the principal estimator and metric. Minor editorial issues—including malformed equation numbering, grammar errors, and the empty demo link—further reduce polish but do not determine the rating.

Overall, the idea is worthwhile and the perceptual results are promising, but the paper's defining claim—physically grounded audio generation—rests on a small, self-referential evaluation without verified physical ground truth or adequate controls. This evidentiary gap currently outweighs the contribution, leading to a weak-reject recommendation rather than a borderline or accept score.

strengths: The paper identifies an important limitation of current video-to-audio systems: semantic and temporal alignment do not guarantee that sound intensity varies consistently with visible physical dynamics.

PAVAS presents a coherent end-to-end design combining object discovery, mass and velocity estimation, object-centric features, and residual physics conditioning. The proposed VGG-Impact subset and APCC metric are potentially useful starting points for studying physical plausibility.

The evaluation includes numerous baselines, conventional objective metrics, a user study, qualitative spectrograms, and ablations. Relative to the comparably sized MMAudio-L baseline, PAVAS-L substantially improves several distributional and semantic metrics.
The manuscript is generally readable, and the system diagrams communicate the pipeline clearly.
weaknesses: The central claim of improved physical grounding is not convincingly isolated. There is no counterfactual experiment that holds the video fixed while varying mass or velocity, and Table 3 omits APCC entirely. Consequently, the reported gains could arise from additional object-centric visual features or capacity rather than meaningful use of the numerical physical quantities.

APCC has serious validity and specification limitations. The predicted mass and velocity used to condition PAVAS are also used to compute the evaluation-side kinetic-energy proxy, creating a favorable and partly circular test. The exact correlation and APCC-difference equations and class aggregation are not given. Moreover, matching a correlation coefficient does not establish calibrated acoustic behavior and can be achieved by a simple monotonic response to the conditioning values.

APCC is evaluated on only 272 impact moments across 10 classes, without per-class counts, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or sensitivity to estimation and onset-detection errors. The metric also conflates physical consistency with onset detection and synchronization, and it is not validated against human physical-plausibility judgments.

The claimed reliability of the Physics Parameter Estimator is essential but unsupported in the provided manuscript: quantitative mass and velocity results are deferred to supplementary material. VLM-based mass guessing and monocular 3D centroid differencing are both error-prone, especially under scale ambiguity, camera motion, occlusion, articulation, and changing visible surfaces; no uncertainty or failure analysis is presented.

The physical model is substantially oversimplified. Impact sound depends on relative velocities, both interacting objects, contact geometry, material, deformation, and acoustic radiation efficiency, whereas the evaluation is described primarily through one object's mass and pre/post-impact kinetic energy. The manuscript does not explain robust association of detected objects, collisions, and audio onsets.

Comparison conditions are uneven: PAVAS-L and MMAudio-L operate at 44.1 kHz, while most baselines operate at 16 kHz, and some results are reproduced while others use author-provided samples. The ablation is conducted only with the smaller 16-kHz backbone. Against the most comparable MMAudio-L model, some gains are marginal or absent, including IS and DeSync.

The user study is too limited to substantiate perceptual superiority: it has only 15 participants, ambiguously states that each rates eight generated audios, and reports no sampling protocol, randomization, significance tests, or confidence intervals. The small mean differences from MMAudio-L should not be interpreted from standard deviations alone.

Reproducibility is weak. VGG-Impact curation and annotation procedures are underspecified, key prompts and implementation details are deferred elsewhere, important architectural hyperparameters are absent, and the manuscript's demo link is visibly missing. Overall, the work has a worthwhile premise, but its defining physics claim lacks sufficiently independent and rigorous evidence, favoring weak rejection.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored limitation of video-to-audio systems: acoustic outputs may be perceptually plausible yet inconsistent with visible physical dynamics. This is a relevant contribution to audiovisual generation and physical scene understanding.

PAVAS presents a coherent object-centric pipeline: a VLM-based mass estimator and segmentation plus dynamic 3D reconstruction provide mass and velocity cues, while the proposed Phy-Adapter injects them through a stable residual modulation mechanism. The design is technically plausible and clearly motivated.

The empirical results are promising. Relative to the closely related MMAudio-L backbone, PAVAS-L improves APCC-Δ from 0.536 to 0.378, FD-PaSST from 60.60 to 47.38, FD-PANNs from 4.72 to 3.99, ImageBind score from 33.22 to 35.41, and user-rated physical plausibility from 3.96 to 4.34.

The additional-training control is valuable: merely training the backbone longer does not reproduce the gains. The mass-only, velocity-only, combined-conditioning, and injection-strategy ablations provide evidence that both physical signals contribute and that residual modulation is preferable to direct summation.

VGG-Impact and APCC address an evaluation dimension largely missed by standard distributional, semantic, and synchronization metrics. The benchmark, quantitative comparisons, user study, and qualitative spectrograms together provide reasonably broad evidence.
The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and easy to follow; the overview diagram communicates the fairly complex system effectively.
weaknesses: The central physical-realism evidence relies almost entirely on the newly proposed APCC-Δ metric over only 272 impact moments and 10 classes. The paper reports neither uncertainty nor statistical significance, although within-class correlations may be unstable with roughly 27 examples per class. It also does not precisely specify the class-wise aggregation or the APCC-Δ formula.

APCC is not an independent validation of physical correctness: it uses the same estimated mass and velocity variables supplied to PAVAS as conditioning. Moreover, acoustic onset strength is affected by material, geometry, contact location, and recording conditions, while kinetic-energy loss is not generally converted directly into radiated sound. Controlled interventions on mass or velocity, or validation against measured physical quantities, would make the physics claim substantially stronger.

The manuscript states that the mass and velocity estimators are comparable to or better than specialized models, but the provided main paper contains no quantitative PPE results, datasets, errors, or failure analysis; these are deferred to supplementary material. Because estimator reliability underpins both conditioning and evaluation, this is a material evidentiary gap in the manuscript provided.

The physics-aware ablation in Table 3 omits APCC-Δ, despite physical consistency being the main claim. It therefore establishes improvements in conventional audio metrics but does not directly isolate whether mass, velocity, or Δ-modulation causes the reported physics-consistency gain.

Some claims overstate the table: PAVAS-L is not better than MMAudio-L on every metric—it is slightly worse on FD-VGG (1.15 versus 0.97) and DeSync (0.446 versus 0.442). Comparisons also mix sampling rates, author-provided samples, reproduced outputs, and methods with or without test-time text, limiting strict comparability.

VGG-Impact construction is insufficiently documented for reproducibility: the paper lacks the complete class composition, impact annotation protocol, annotator agreement, event-selection rules, and release details. The user study likewise gives only 15 participants and does not clearly report the number and sampling of evaluated clips, repeated-measures protocol, or significance tests.

The practical cost is obscured. Inference requires several large pretrained components, including a VLM, Florence-2, SAM2, and CUT3R, yet Table 1's parameter accounting largely excludes pretrained modules and no latency, memory, or estimator runtime is reported. This matters for the method's potential usefulness, although it does not negate the scientific contribution.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored limitation of video-to-audio systems: semantic and temporal plausibility do not guarantee that sound intensity varies consistently with visible dynamics.

PAVAS is a coherent engineering contribution. It combines open-vocabulary object discovery, segmentation, dynamic 3D reconstruction, mass estimation, and gated residual conditioning in a technically plausible pipeline. The zero-initialized delta-modulation design is sensible for adding conditions to a pretrained generator.

Against the strongest comparable baseline, MMAudio-L, PAVAS-L improves most conventional metrics, including FD-PaSST (60.60 to 47.38), FD-PANNs (4.72 to 3.99), KL, ImageBind score (33.22 to 35.41), and human ratings, while roughly preserving DeSync.

The supplementary material is unusually substantial: it provides full prompts, architectures, training settings, runtime profiling, perturbation and missing-cue tests, estimator evaluations, and impact/non-impact results. The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished.
weaknesses: The central evidence for physical realism is not technically convincing. APCC uses physical quantities estimated by the same PPE that conditions PAVAS, rather than independently measured ground truth, creating a self-referential evaluation. Its kinetic-energy proxy uses one object's centroid speed rather than relative/contact-normal velocity and effective mass of both bodies, and omits material, contact geometry, microphone gain, and source distance, all of which strongly affect onset energy.

The APCC definition is ambiguous and potentially ill-posed: the paper says that energy and onset-strength sequences are z-normalized per video but that Pearson correlation is computed per class, without specifying how videos and multiple onsets are pooled or associated. Per-video normalization also removes any constant mass scaling within a clip, so the proposed metric cannot directly validate the claimed effect of mass. Detecting onsets from generated audio and sampling video energy around those generated onset times further entangles physical plausibility with onset timing.

APCC-Delta only matches a class-level correlation coefficient to the ground-truth correlation. A generator can obtain a similar correlation while producing incorrectly calibrated or event-wise mismatched sounds, and closeness to a potentially weak ground-truth correlation does not establish physical correctness. The shuffling/noise checks show sensitivity to the PPE values but do not establish perceptual validity or resistance to such degenerate solutions.

The key causal ablation is missing. Table 3 does not report APCC for mass-only, velocity-only, no-physics, or direct-summation variants. Moreover, every physics branch is constructed by modulating object-centric visual features, but there is no object-feature-only control. Consequently, the reported perceptual gains cannot be attributed specifically to numerical mass and velocity rather than additional object masks/features and fine-tuning.

Estimator validation is weaker than claimed. Velocity is evaluated on only 256 manually filtered clips against another pretrained-model pipeline's pseudo-ground truth, not measured velocity, and only tolerance-bar plots are given. The actual operating pipeline replaces 65.15% of Grounded-SAM2 frame observations with occlusion tokens, which conflicts with the characterization that missing observations are limited and raises questions about how often usable velocity conditioning exists.

VGG-Impact is small (272 moments over 10 classes), manually selected partly according to successful masks, and lacks reported class counts, released annotations, annotation agreement, or uncertainty estimates. The human study similarly uses only eight filtered clips and reports no confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or participant-level analysis, despite presenting small mean differences as favorable evidence.

Some comparisons are confounded by sample rate and evaluation source: most baselines operate at 16 kHz whereas PAVAS-L operates at 44.1 kHz, and results mix reproduced outputs with author-provided samples. The fair MMAudio-L comparison remains useful, but it does not repair the missing causal evidence for physical grounding.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the detailed supplement: exact VGG-Impact membership/event annotations, precise APCC pooling and event-object matching, Fourier frequencies, complete training-corpus composition, random seeds, and code/model-release information are not provided. These are material for reproducing the principal claim, rather than presentation-only refinements.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored limitation of video-to-audio systems: sounds can be semantically and temporally appropriate while remaining inconsistent with visible object dynamics. The proposed VGG-Impact subset and emphasis on physical plausibility are potentially useful directions for the community.

PAVAS is a coherent end-to-end system. It combines open-vocabulary object discovery, segmentation, dynamic 3D reconstruction, mass estimation, object-centric features, and gated AdaLN conditioning in a technically plausible way. The manuscript also provides useful implementation details, prompts, runtime measurements, missing-observation handling, and training configurations.

Against the strongest comparable baseline, MMAudio-L, PAVAS-L improves several conventional metrics, including FD-PaSST (60.60 to 47.38), FD-PANNs (4.72 to 3.99), KL, and ImageBind similarity (33.22 to 35.41), while approximately preserving DeSync. The comparison on impact and non-impact subsets also suggests that the gains are not confined to the curated benchmark.

The paper includes component ablations, inference-time perturbation tests, a missing-cue fallback experiment, auxiliary evaluations of mass and displacement estimation, and a user study. These are broader than a purely benchmark-driven evaluation and show that the system does not fail abruptly when its physical inputs are missing.
weaknesses: The central APCC evaluation has serious conceptual and specification problems. The paper says that kinetic-energy changes and onset strengths are z-normalized for each video and then correlated per class, but it does not define how per-video sequences are combined or handle videos with only one event, for which z-normalization and Pearson correlation are undefined. Class-wise sample counts, uncertainty, and confidence intervals are also absent. Consequently, the reported APCC-Delta values cannot be independently interpreted or reproduced from the manuscript.

APCC does not substantiate the claimed sensitivity to mass. Within a video and object, the estimated mass is a constant multiplicative factor in every kinetic-energy value; per-video z-normalization removes that factor. Thus, the headline physics metric is effectively insensitive to the mass cue that constitutes one of the paper's two principal physical variables. More generally, acoustic onset strength is affected by material, contact geometry, microphone distance, and room acoustics, so correlation with estimated kinetic-energy loss alone is not strong evidence of physical correctness.

The evaluation is circular in important respects: APCC uses the authors' own estimated masses, velocities, masks, and onset associations rather than measured physical quantities, and VGG-Impact explicitly removes clips whose masks or tracks are unreliable. The shuffle and noise tests only establish sensitivity to perturbations of this estimator-derived signal; they do not validate that APCC agrees with real physical parameters or human judgments of controlled physical changes.

The decisive causal ablations are missing. Table 3 evaluates only conventional perceptual metrics, not APCC, and never compares against shuffled, constant, or random mass/velocity values. Moreover, both the mass and velocity branches modulate object-centric visual features, so their gains could arise from segmentation-derived object features or additional capacity rather than the numerical physical values. There is no visual-feature-only control or oracle-physics experiment. Therefore, the experiments do not establish that explicit physical quantities cause the reported APCC or quality improvements.

The physical estimators are not validated adequately for the in-the-wild setting in which they are used. Mass is evaluated on 500 product objects from ABO rather than dynamic VGGSound scenes. Velocity is evaluated against a pseudo-ground-truth construction pipeline on a manually filtered subset, with only tolerance plots and no numerical errors or direct metric-velocity ground truth. The paper nevertheless describes these estimates as reliable and metric-scale. This overstates what the evidence supports, especially given that 65.15% of segmentation frames reportedly receive occlusion tokens.

Evidence for controllable physical behavior is mostly qualitative. The claimed controlled mass and velocity manipulations appear only as supplementary demonstrations; there is no systematic test that generated loudness or spectral energy changes monotonically with controlled mass or speed while appearance, event identity, and random seed are held fixed. Such an experiment is essential for distinguishing learned physical control from ordinary appearance-conditioned generation.

The user study is too limited to strongly support broad perceptual claims: it uses only eight manually selected, non-ambiguous clips, 27 participants, and reports means and standard deviations without paired significance tests, confidence intervals, or participant-level analysis. Since the same clips and models are repeatedly rated, treating the resulting ratings as independent would also be inappropriate.

Some conventional comparisons are difficult to interpret because most baselines operate at 16 kHz while PAVAS-L and MMAudio-L operate at 44.1 kHz, and results mix locally reproduced outputs with author-provided samples. The direct comparison with MMAudio-L is useful, but PAVAS is additionally fine-tuned on VGGSound and the main table does not isolate that training difference at the large-model scale. PAVAS also slightly worsens FD-VGG and DeSync relative to MMAudio-L.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the detailed architecture description. The exact VGG-Impact clip/event list, event-to-object association procedure, APCC aggregation implementation, evaluation seeds, and full training-data composition are not provided. Mass inference uses stochastic VLM decoding, but the number of samples, seed, and aggregation rule are unspecified. These omissions affect the paper's central benchmark and physical-conditioning inputs rather than merely presentation.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/c71a1163ab454983a35ea323fdb28861/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} identifies an important and underexplored limitation of video-to-audio systems: semantic and temporal plausibility do not guarantee that acoustic intensity varies consistently with visible dynamics. Conditioning generation on object-level mass and velocity is a useful and original direction.

The proposed pipeline is technically coherent: open-vocabulary detection and segmentation, dynamic 3D reconstruction, object-centric features, Fourier embeddings, FiLM modulation, and zero-initialized gated AdaLN residuals form a plausible end-to-end design. The residual physics-injection mechanism is particularly sensible for preserving a pretrained multimodal pathway.

Reported general-generation results are strong. Relative to MMAudio-L, PAVAS-L improves FD-PaSST from 60.60 to 47.38, FD-PANNs from 4.72 to 3.99, ImageBind similarity from 33.22 to 35.41, and several KL/IS measures, while approximately preserving synchronization; it also performs favorably in the 27-participant study.

The paper supplies useful component validation and robustness analysis: mass is evaluated on ABO-500, velocity on a filtered STARSS23 proxy, missing-cue fallback is tested, and perturbation experiments show gradual degradation. Reporting runtime and missing-observation statistics is also valuable.

Presentation and reproducibility are generally good. The architecture, prompts, model variants, training schedule, hardware, preprocessing, occlusion handling, metric equations, and user-study questions are described in substantial detail.
weaknesses: The principal physics evidence is not sufficiently independent. PAVAS is conditioned on mass and velocity produced by PPE, while APCC is defined using physical quantities produced by that same PPE. VGG-Impact additionally removes examples whose PPE masks are unreliable. Consequently, the headline APCC result primarily shows agreement with the model's own selected conditioning signal, not necessarily agreement with independently measured real-world physics.

No ablation reports APCC. Table 3 evaluates mass-only, velocity-only, combined conditioning, and the injection strategy solely with conventional perceptual metrics. Thus, the manuscript does not directly demonstrate that either physical variable or the proposed adapter causes the claimed improvement in physical consistency. This missing causal evidence is material to the central contribution.

APCC has unresolved validity and specification issues. It measures only a class-level correlation difference rather than per-event physical accuracy; a model could match the ground-truth correlation while producing incorrectly scaled sounds. Ground-truth class correlations, class sample counts, uncertainty intervals, and results over generation seeds are omitted. Moreover, the stated per-video z-normalization would remove any constant multiplicative mass effect within a video and may be ill-defined for clips with very few impacts, undermining the claim that APCC validates mass-aware synthesis.

The physics model is simplified and the estimator validation is only indirect. Impact acoustics also depend strongly on material, contact geometry, elasticity, damping, and environment. Velocity is evaluated against another model-derived displacement pipeline on 256 manually filtered clips rather than measured velocity, while the reported figure lacks exact numerical values. These limitations make the language about metric-scale, physically grounded behavior stronger than the evidence supports.

The subjective evaluation is encouraging but narrow: it uses only eight selectively filtered non-speech clips, provides no statistical significance or participant-level analysis, and does not report safeguards such as headphone checks. Dataset sizes for the large audio-text training corpora, random-seed variability, APCC annotation release details, and uncertainty for quantitative comparisons are also missing. Overall, the method is promising and potentially useful, but the lack of an independent and ablated validation of its defining physics claim keeps the recommendation at the decision boundary.
